analysis.one_liner: Sets safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials, including two-person crews, speed limits, defect detectors, and higher fines.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 2, 2026 with 13 cosponsors split evenly between parties, then referred to two House committees and its railroads subcommittee, where it sits with no markup or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require freight railroads to run two-person crews, slow trains carrying flammable and toxic materials, install networks of trackside detectors that catch failing equipment before it causes a derailment, and share real-time lists of what hazardous chemicals are on each train with firefighters and police. It would force older tank cars out of flammable-liquid service, raise fines for safety violations to as much as $5 million, and fund protective gear and emergency-response grants for the communities along freight routes.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and drive along freight rail routes: communities that could be hit by a derailment, drivers stuck at blocked crossings, first responders who need to know what chemicals are on a burning train, and rail employees who perform safety inspections and operate trains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Railside communities, first responders, rail workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires a minimum two-person crew on Class I freight trains, with no exception for high-hazard trains or trains longer than 7,500 feet, and bars railroads from limiting the time employees need to complete safety inspections.

Caps most trains at 50 mph and high-hazard flammable-liquid trains at 40 mph in designated high-threat urban areas, and requires buffer cars between locomotives and hazardous tank cars to reduce derailment severity.

Requires Class I railroads to build defect detector networks that catch overheated wheel bearings and other failures before they cause accidents, including detectors placed so trains are scanned before entering urbanized areas of 75,000 or more people.

Requires railroads to generate real-time electronic train consist information — what hazardous materials are on board, where — and share it with fusion centers, state emergency commissions, and first responders, and bars them from withholding it during an emergency.

Raises civil penalties for rail safety violations to between $5,000 and $1 million per day, up to $5 million when a violation causes death, serious injury, or major property destruction, and allows doubling for repeat or willful violations.
Bars older tank cars from carrying flammable liquids after December 31, 2027 unless they meet modern DOT-117 safety standards, with a possible one-year delay if manufacturers cannot keep up.

Requires every railroad to run a toll-free hotline for reporting blocked highway-rail grade crossings, gives school-bus routes priority in the federal crossing-elimination program, and funds a National Academy study of the most-blocked crossings.

Expands hazardous materials emergency preparedness grants so local departments can buy protective equipment, and creates a program that can release up to $10 million quickly to communities responding to a serious hazmat transportation incident.

analysis.who_pays: Class I freight railroads bear most of the cost: detector networks, two-person crews, tank car upgrades, emergency plans, and larger fines. Companies that ship or register hazardous materials pay annual registration fees of up to $5,000, and some compliance costs could ultimately show up in freight prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class I railroads and hazmat shippers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: detector networks, two-person crews on every train, and a tank car phase-out are significant expenses for railroads, and railroads and shippers argue some of that lands in freight rates paid by businesses and consumers.

The bill is softer than a full mandate in places: trains that already ran with fewer than two people a year before enactment are exempt unless the Secretary finds they are less safe, railroads can seek waivers, and the tank car phase-out can be pushed to 2028 if manufacturing capacity falls short.

Several provisions only direct studies and reports — a National Academy review of blocked crossings, GAO reviews of worker protections and of the Federal Railroad Administration's own workforce — which produce information rather than immediate safety changes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains target documented failure modes — overheated bearings, thin crews, older tank cars, and first responders arriving without knowing what is on a derailed train — and the bill builds in flexibility (waivers, small-business carve-outs, a possible phase-out delay) that softens the cost argument. The main honest cost is that hauling hazardous freight would get more expensive, and the bill's many study-and-report provisions mean some of it would take years to change anything even if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2026 and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Science committees, then to the Railroads Subcommittee, where it sits with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the bill on March 2, 2026, joined from the start by Reps. LaLota, Garamendi, and Rulli.
It was referred the same day to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, for the provisions in its jurisdiction, the Science, Space, and Technology Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where it has remained with no further action.
It has 13 cosponsors, 7 Republicans and 6 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Class I freight railroads, which continue operating under current rules while the bill sits in subcommittee, avoiding the costs of detector networks, two-person crews, and the tank car phase-out it would impose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Class I freight railroads, for now

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.what_they_did: The industry opposed similar rail-safety mandates, including the prior Railway Safety Act and federal crew-size rules, and pressed against their cost.

sides.party_line_note: Support is genuinely split: two of the four original sponsors are Republicans, and the 13 cosponsors divide 7 Republican and 6 Democrat, with no opposition vote on record yet because the bill has not reached one.

industries.note: The bill's costs fall squarely on the largest freight railroads: detector networks on main lines, two-person crews, speed caps, tank car upgrades, real-time consist sharing, emergency plans, and fines up to $5 million per violation. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs directly against the safety of the communities their trains pass through.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and retrofit shops
industries.note: The December 2027 phase-out of older tank cars from flammable-liquid service creates a wave of demand for new DOT-117 cars and retrofits, and the bill funds tank car research. Building safer cars is the same work that keeps hazardous cargo from rupturing in a derailment.

The two-person crew minimum, the ban on limiting inspection time, audit requirements checking whether managers pressure employees to sign off on inspections, and drug-and-alcohol testing for inspection staff all add protections for rail workers that double as safety protections for the public.

industries.industry: Fire departments and local emergency responders
industries.note: Larger emergency preparedness grants, permission to buy protective equipment with grant funds, paid training time for volunteers, and a fast-release fund of up to $10 million for communities hit by a serious hazmat incident all flow to the local responders who arrive first at a derailment.

Non-small-business registrants pay an annual fee of up to $5,000 to fund the emergency preparedness system. The cost is modest, and the money goes to the first-response capacity that protects the same communities these shipments pass through.

analysis.trajectory: Most House bills die in committee without a vote, and a subcommittee referral with no scheduled hearing is the usual resting place. This one's rare bipartisan sponsorship and continued public attention to hazmat derailments give it a better chance than most, but it still needs the Transportation and Infrastructure chair to schedule a markup and a committee vote before any floor action — which has not happened.
